newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan key rate seen flat amid tax rises.
newsitem.headline: Japan key rate seen flat amid tax rises.

text.p: Japan's key interest rate is likely to be kept at its record low level at least until the end of June as tax increases from April 1 slow economic recovery, economists said in a Reuters poll released on Thursday.

Of 28 economists at research institutes, banks and brokerages who responded to the poll, all but one expected the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to leave its official discount rate unchanged at 0.5 percent until the end of June. The central bank charges the rate on loans to commercial banks.
The economists said a rise in the consumption tax to five percent from three percent and an end to special income tax cuts in the fiscal year starting in April could stall the economic recovery.

"The pace of the recovery is likely to slow down in the April-June period, albeit temporarily, reflecting a rush to buy ahead of the tax rises," said Manabu Kondo, senior researcher at Sakura Institute of Research.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's proposed tight budget for fiscal 1997/98, which includes the tax moves and a cut in public spending, will be a key factor weakening the strength of the recovery, they said.

The Tokyo stock market has been in a downtrend since the 1997/98 budget was unveiled late last year. The key Nikkei index closed on Thursday at 17,909.46 points, compared with a close of 19,446.00 on January 6, its first trading day of the year.
The budget, which aims at getting Japan's big budget deficit under control, needs approval from parliament, which convened on Monday.
The survey covered 37 brokerages and research bodies, although not all those polled responded to all the questions.

Kondo and five other economists said the BOJ may raise its key lending rate by between 0.25 and 0.50 percentage points by the end of September because corporate sentiment is likely to have picked up after the financial markets discount the negative impact from the fiscal tightening.
Takao Hattori, an economist at Dai-Ichi Research and Management Institute, said current economic data is strong enough for the central bank to push up the discount rate to 1.0 percent.
But market sentiment is lagging behind actual economic conditions, forcing the BOJ to maintain the lower rate.
"The BOJ may raise the discount rate to the theoretically appropriate one percent level in the latter half of the July-September period," said Hattori.
"Market operators may realise their outlook of the economy was much worse than the reality after they overcome the one-time shocks of the tax rises," Hattori said.

BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita lent some support to that view on Monday, telling a central bank branch managers' meeting that Japan's economy was still gradually recovering and that the strength of the recovery was growing gradually.
Concerning the BOJ's current monetary policy, Matsushita said: "We think it is appropriate to continue careful watch over developments and put emphasis on securing the basis for economic recovery."

Of the 25 economists willing to predict what the discount rate would be at the end of March 1998, 13 expected it to be between 1.0 and 2.0 percent by then, while 12 said the rate would still be at 0.5 percent.
The survey was conducted between January 13 and 16.
